q: 326. The stress-strain curve of an over consolidated clay is similar to that of .............
explain: Over-consolidated clay shows peak-strength, dilative behaviour under shear similar to dense sand.

q: 327. The stress-strain curve of a normal consolidated clay is similar to that of .............
explain: Normally consolidated clay shows a gradually rising, contractive stress-strain curve similar to loose sand.

q: 328. In the triaxial test, the intermediate principal stress will be equal to .............
options: average of major and minor principal stresses
explain: In a standard (axisymmetric) triaxial test, cell pressure acts equally on all lateral directions, so the intermediate principal stress equals the minor (confining) stress.

q: 329. Vane shear test is a .............
options: can be done both in field and laboratory
explain: The vane shear test can be performed both in-situ in the field and on samples in the laboratory.

q: 330. When the plastic limit is equal to or greater than the liquid limit, then the plasticity index is .............
explain: By convention, plasticity index is reported as zero (not negative) when PL >= LL, since PI = LL - PL cannot be negative.

q: 331. The shrinkage index is equal to .............
explain: Per the reference key, shrinkage index is expressed as liquid limit minus shrinkage limit in this classification.

q: 332. The flow index in soils indicates the .............
options: ratio of liquid limit to plastic limit
shear strength variation with water content
explain: Flow index reflects how shear strength (resistance to flow) changes with water content, based on the liquid limit test's flow curve.

q: 333. The clays which exhibit high activity .............
explain: Highly active clays typically both contain montmorillonite and exhibit high plasticity index, since activity relates PI to clay fraction.

q: 334. The activity of clay is defined as the ratio of .............
explain: Skempton's activity is defined as plasticity index divided by the percentage of clay-sized (<2 micron) fraction.

q: 335. The ratio of the liquid limit minus the natural content of a soil to its plasticity index, is known as .............
explain: This ratio, (LL - w)/PI, defines relative consistency (also related to consistency index).

q: 336. When the particles of soil are oriented 'edge to edge' or 'edge to face' with respect to one another, the soil is said to have .............
explain: Edge-to-edge or edge-to-face particle orientation, common in clay deposition, produces a loose, open flocculent structure.

q: 337. The pressure exerted by water on the soil through which it percolates, is known as .............
explain: The drag force exerted by percolating (seeping) water on soil grains is termed seepage pressure.

q: 338. The equi-potential line in a seepage through a soil medium is defined as the .............
options: path of particles of water through a saturated soil mass
line connecting points of equal head of water
flow of movement of fine particles of soil
explain: An equipotential line connects all points in the seepage domain that share the same total head.

q: 339. The exit gradient of the seepage of water through a soil medium is the .............
options: ratio of total head to the length of seepage
ratio of the head loss to the length of seepage
explain: Exit gradient is defined as the head loss per unit length at the point where seepage exits the soil, i.e., head loss over seepage path length.

q: 340. The phenomenon in which a cohesion less soil loses all its shear strength and the soil particles have a tendency to move up in the direction of flow, is known as .............
explain: Boiling condition, quicksand, and quick condition are all terms used interchangeably for this loss of effective stress under upward seepage.

q: 341. If the pores of a soil are completely full of air only, the soil is said to be .............
explain: A soil with only air (no water) in its voids is classified as dry soil.

q: 342. The ratio of the volume of voids to the total volume of soil mass is called .............
explain: Porosity is defined as the ratio of void volume to the total volume of the soil mass.

q: 343. The ratio of the unit weight of soil solids to that of water is called .............
explain: Specific gravity of soil solids is defined as the ratio of the unit weight of solids to the unit weight of water.

q: 344. The unit weight of a soil at zero air voids depends upon .............
explain: The zero-air-voids unit weight formula combines unit weight of water, water content, and specific gravity of solids together.

q: 345. Bentonite contains predominantly .............
explain: Bentonite is a clay predominantly composed of montmorillonite, giving it its characteristic high swelling capacity.

options: mixture of sand, silt and clay sized particles in equal proportions
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'silt with little sand'; loam is more commonly defined (as seen earlier for Q10) as a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay.

q: 347. Compressibility of a clayey soils will be .............
options: equal to that of sandy soils
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'equal to sandy soils'; the standard geotechnical fact is that clayey soils are typically far more compressible than sandy soils.

q: 348. The co-efficient of compressibility of an over consolidated clay will be .............
options: equal to that of a normally consolidated clay
greater than that of a normally consolidated clay
less than that of a normally consolidated clay
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'equal to'; standard geotechnical understanding is that over-consolidated clay has a lower compressibility coefficient than normally consolidated clay at the same stress increment (within the recompression range).

q: 349. Shearing strength of cohesionless soil depends upon .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'loading rate'; shear strength of cohesionless soils is more classically governed by density/void ratio and normal stress via the friction angle.

q: 350. Rise in the water table position upto the ground surface causes .............
explain: A rising water table increases pore water pressure and total stress at a given point, while effective stress typically decreases due to buoyant unit weight replacing dry/moist unit weight.

q: 351. The maximum size of grains of silts is about .............
explain: The upper size boundary for silt-sized particles (below fine sand) is conventionally taken as about 0.06 mm (per some classification systems).

options: soil composed of two different soils
fine grained soil with little or no plasticity
clay with a high percentage of the clay mineral
explain: Silt is defined as a fine-grained soil that exhibits little to no plasticity, distinguishing it from clay.

q: 353. Black cotton soil .............
options: contains large percentage of clay mineral
explain: Black cotton soil is inorganic, rich in montmorillonite clay, and highly compressible/expansive — all these characteristics apply.

q: 354. A fine grained soil .............
options: may or may not be plastic
explain: Fine-grained soils generally exhibit low permeability, high compressibility, and variable plasticity (from non-plastic silt to highly plastic clay) — all apply.

q: 355. Electrical analogy method is used to .............
options: find the depth to water table
find the water content in a soil
explain: The electrical analogy method uses the similarity between Darcy's and Ohm's laws to experimentally construct flow nets.

q: 356. The space factor of a flow net is defined as .............
explain: The space (shape) factor of a flow net is defined as the ratio of number of flow channels to number of equipotential drops, Nf/Nd.

q: 357. Find out the correct statement about shape factor .............
explain: The shape factor of a flow net depends only on geometry, not on the permeability value of the soil.

q: 358. The u/s face of an earth dam is .............
explain: The upstream (submerged) face of an earth dam, being in contact with reservoir water at constant head, acts as an equipotential line.

q: 359. The top flow line in the case of seepage flow through an earth dam has the shape of .............
explain: The phreatic (top flow) line through a homogeneous earth dam closely approximates a parabola (Casagrande's method).

q: 360. Flow through an earth dam is a case of .............
explain: Seepage through an earth dam has a free (phreatic) surface exposed to atmospheric pressure, characterizing unconfined flow.

q: 361. The pheriatic line is .............
options: the u/s face of the earth dam
d/s face of the earth dam
explain: The phreatic line is defined as the top flow line (free surface) of seepage through an earth dam.

options: a condition in which cohesion is decreased quickly
a sand which can act as a quick filter
condition in which cohesion less soil looses its shear strength due to upward flow of water
explain: Quicksand describes the condition where upward seepage force equals or exceeds submerged weight, eliminating effective stress and shear strength in cohesionless soil.

q: 363. The quantity of seepage in a soil is .............
options: directly proportional to the coefficient of permeability
inversely proportional to the coefficient of permeability
directly proportional to the uniformity coefficient of the soil
explain: By Darcy's law, seepage discharge is directly proportional to permeability (q = kiA).

q: 364. Flow net consists of a number of stream lines and equipotential lines which are .............
explain: Flow lines and equipotential lines in a flow net are drawn orthogonal (at right angles) to each other by construction.

q: 365. The seepage force in a soil is .............
explain: Seepage force acts in the direction of flow, which is perpendicular to the equipotential lines.

q: 366. The seepage force in soils at exit is proportional to .............
options: the head of water at d/s
the head of water at u/s
explain: Seepage force per unit volume at the exit point is directly proportional to the exit hydraulic gradient.

q: 367. Flow net is used for the determination of .............
explain: A flow net simultaneously allows determination of exit gradient, total seepage quantity, and pore/hydrostatic pressures at any point.

q: 368. The symbol CL indicates .............
explain: In USCS notation, CL denotes inorganic clay of low to medium plasticity.

q: 369. The symbol OH indicates .............
options: organic silts and organic silts of high plasticity
explain: In USCS notation, OH denotes organic clay/silt of high plasticity.

q: 370. Peat is nothing but .............
explain: Per the reference key, peat is classified here as organic clay, reflecting its high organic decomposed plant matter content.

q: 371. Generally, when compacted the GW type of soils will be .............
explain: Even when well compacted, well-graded gravel (GW) retains interconnected voids large enough to remain pervious.

q: 372. A soil which is fully consolidated under the existing over burden pressure is known as .............
explain: A soil fully consolidated under its present overburden (with no excess pore pressure remaining) is defined as normally consolidated.

q: 373. Secondary consolidation of soil is due to the expulsion of .............
explain: Secondary consolidation involves slow expulsion of tightly bound (adsorbed) water and plastic readjustment of soil structure, distinct from primary consolidation's free water expulsion.

q: 374. The relationship between the time factor Tv, coefficient of consolidation Cv, the length of drainage path d, and time t is given by .............
explain: Time factor is defined as Tv = Cv.t/d^2, a dimensionless parameter combining consolidation coefficient, time, and drainage path length.

q: 375. The time factor for a particular degree of consolidation .............
options: depends upon the coefficient of consolidation
depends upon the distribution of initial excess hydrostatic pressure
explain: For a given degree of consolidation, the time factor Tv depends on the shape of the initial excess pore pressure distribution across the layer.

q: 376. The compression resulting from long term static load and resulting expulsion of water is known as .............
explain: Consolidation is precisely the gradual volume reduction from long-term static load causing pore water expulsion.

q: 377. Compression of soils occurs rapidly if voids are occupied by .............
explain: Air is highly compressible and escapes voids almost instantly under load, so soils with air-filled voids compress much faster than saturated soils.

q: 378. The compressibility of a field deposit is .............
options: the same as that shown by a laboratory sample
greater than that shown by a laboratory sample
smaller than that shown by a laboratory sample
explain: Field deposits often contain natural discontinuities/fissures and larger-scale heterogeneity, making them generally more compressible than small intact lab samples.

q: 379. Mathematically speaking, the time taken for 100% consolidation is .............
explain: Terzaghi's consolidation theory is an exponential/asymptotic process, so 100% consolidation is mathematically reached only at infinite time.

q: 380. If consolidation experiments are conducted on two soil samples of the same soil but having different thickness (thick and thin) then the deformations will be higher in .............
explain: Total settlement is proportional to layer thickness under the same effective stress increment, so the thicker sample undergoes greater overall deformation.

q: 381. As the length of drainage path increases the time required for consolidation .............
explain: Since time factor Tv = Cv.t/d^2, a longer drainage path (d) requires proportionally more time (as d^2) to reach the same degree of consolidation.

q: 382. The ratio of settlement at any time t, to the final settlement is called as .............
explain: Degree of consolidation (Uz) is defined as the ratio of settlement achieved at time t to the eventual final (total) settlement.

q: 383. A clay deposit subjected to pressure in the past which is more than the present overburden pressure is known as .............
explain: When past pressure exceeded the present overburden, the clay is classified as over-consolidated (OCR > 1).

q: 384. A clay deposit which is not fully consolidated under the existing over burden pressure is known as .............
explain: A deposit still consolidating under its current overburden (excess pore pressure not fully dissipated) is termed under-consolidated.

q: 385. Falling head permeameter is preferable when soil sample is .............
explain: Falling head permeameters are suited for low-permeability (clayey) soils, where flow rates are too slow for the constant head method to measure accurately.

q: 386. In the case of stratified soils, the permeabilities Kx and Kz along and across stratification are related as .............
options: no relation between Kx and Kz
explain: Stratified soils have higher permeability parallel to layering (Kx, horizontal) than across it (Kz, vertical), since flow along layers avoids crossing low-permeability lenses.

q: 387. The range of coefficient of permeability of sands is about .............
explain: Sands typically have permeability in the range of 10^-2 to 10^-4 cm/s, higher than silts and clays.

q: 388. The neutral stress on the soil is due to .............
options: Weight of water present in soil pores
external load acting on the soil
explain: Neutral stress (pore water pressure) is caused by the water present in the soil voids, exerting hydrostatic pressure on grains.

q: 389. When a shear stress is applied on a dense sand, then the volume of sand will .............
explain: Dense sand dilates (increases in volume) under shear as densely packed grains ride over one another.

q: 390. Sensitivity of a clayey soil is defined as .............
options: ratio of strength of an undisturbed soil sample to that of a remoulded sample
ratio of strength of remoulded soil sample to that of an undisturbed soil sample
ratio of deviator load to cross sectional area
explain: Sensitivity is defined as undisturbed strength divided by remoulded strength, quantifying strength loss upon disturbance.
